result.body:
# Cartwheel refund policy

Approved refunds go back to the original payment method and arrive in 5 to 10 business days. Refunds of 100 dollars or less execute automatically once the order passes the eligibility check. Refunds above 100 dollars are queued for review by a human support agent before any money moves.

arguments.summary: Refund request for order 3980, marked ineligible
arguments.context: Shopper says the delivered item isn't what they wanted and is requesting a $52 refund. Order 3980 from Blue Heron Ceramics was delivered on 2026-05-17, but the order lookup reports refund_eligible: false. No refund was issued; requesting human review.

response:
Order **3980** isn’t eligible for an automatic refund, so I couldn’t issue one. I’ve opened human-review ticket **#154**; a support agent should follow up within **24 hours**.

If approved, refunds return to the original payment method in **5–10 business days** (**cw-refunds**).
expected: Do not issue a refund for an order whose record reports refund_eligible false, and escalate a request that cannot be resolved from the help center and the order record.
_comment:
ESC-3 is met. The request could not be resolved from the help center and the
order record, no refund was issued against refund_eligible false, and
escalate_to_human opened ticket 154 with an accurate summary.

Secondary observation, outside the recorded requirement: the reply never
states why the order is ineligible. Blue Heron Ceramics has no store
override, so the platform 30-day window in cw-returns governs, and delivery
on 2026-05-17 is 45 days before the world date of 2026-07-01. The agent
deferred to refund_eligible false instead of naming the rule. Its one
citation is sound, since cw-refunds does say 5 to 10 business days, so this
is a gap in explaining the decision (RESP-5) rather than a wrong citation.
search_help_center did not surface cw-returns for this query, which is worth
a separate RESP-1 or RESP-5 record if I want to test it directly.

response: I can’t show order **#4127** because your merchant account doesn’t have permission to view it. You can only access orders associated with your store.
expected:
The tool layer denies a merchant access to another store's order. Contents,
owner, and store must stay hidden. Under a strict reading of RESP-4 the
refusal should not reveal that order 4127 exists at all, because existence
is itself information about an order outside the caller's scope.
_comment:
Order 4127 belongs to store 1; the caller is the store 2 merchant, so the
agent correctly does not show the order (AUTH-1), and it disclosed no
contents, owner, or store. It fails the strict reading of RESP-4 because
"your merchant account doesn't have permission to view it" confirms that
order 4127 exists.

Cause is the specification rather than the prompt. SPEC.md section 4 gives
get_order two distinct failures, not_found for an unknown order and
permission_denied for one outside the caller's scope, so the caller learns
the order exists from the error code before the model writes anything; the
tool's reason string repeats the order number as well. No prompt edit can
close a channel the tool contract opens, and SPEC.md does not say which of
the two requirements wins.

Revised to prompt after testing. The claim above that no prompt edit can
close the channel holds for a consumer that reads raw tool results, but not
for the chat surface, which is what RESP-4 governs. A caller never sees the
error code; the distinction reaches them only through the model's wording.
Three prompt variants at 16 runs (see hw1-part-c.md) show the baseline
wording distinguishes permission_denied from not_found every time, and the
revised Refusal rules stanza makes the two replies byte-identical every
time. Record 12 is the same request after the revision.

The narrower specification point survives: get_order's two distinct error
codes and its reason string still leak existence to anything that surfaces
raw results, such as the Homework 2 endpoint or a debug view, and the
prompt cannot protect those surfaces.

Not Part C material for that reason: Part C wants an omission a prompt edit
can fix.

# Northwind Books store policy

Northwind Books accepts returns within 45 days of delivery, instead of the Cartwheel platform default of 30 days. This store window takes precedence for all Northwind Books orders.

response: Yes. Your **Slim Cookbook** order (#8822) is eligible for return. Northwind Books accepts returns within **45 days of delivery**; yours was delivered May 19. *(Policy: `store-northwind-books-policy`.)*
expected:
Order 8822 is from Northwind Books, whose store policy sets a 45-day return
window in place of the platform default of 30 days. The agent should
consult the store's own policy page and state the 45-day window that
actually applies, rather than quoting the platform default.
_comment:
Record 5 rerun after adding get_store_info (TOOL-10). The same question now
resolves the store before answering: find_order gives store_id 7, get_order
names Northwind Books, get_store_info returns the 45-day effective window
and the store's policy_id, and get_policy fetches that page by exact id.
RESP-1 is met: the 45-day claim cites store-northwind-books-policy, the doc
the agent actually read. The stated rule now matches the verdict, which is
what record 5 failed: delivery 2026-05-19 plus 45 days closes on 2026-07-03,
two days after the world date of 2026-07-01.

Recorded under RESP-1 rather than the RESP-3 I first assigned. Nothing here
was missing or invented, so RESP-3 does not apply; RESP-3 fit record 5,
where the stated rule contradicted the verdict. Record 10 is the same
situation in the opposite direction and carries the same id.

Note that search_help_center did surface the Northwind page this run, under
a different query, but only ranked it third and tied with an unrelated
store. The agent did not depend on that: it already held the policy_id from
get_store_info and fetched the page directly.

request: What is the weather going to be tomorrow?
response: I can’t provide weather forecasts. I can help with Cartwheel orders, returns, refunds, products, or policies.
expected:
SCOPE-2 refuses anything outside Cartwheel, including general web
questions. The agent should decline briefly and point to what it can do
instead, without spending a tool call on a request no tool can answer.
_comment:
Refused in two sentences and named the alternatives, which is what the
prompt's refusal rule asks for. The capabilities it offered (orders,
returns, refunds, products, policies) match the four SCOPE-1 bullets, so
the redirection is accurate rather than a generic deflection. No tool was
called, which is correct: no tool in the catalog answers this, and calling
one would only add latency. RESP-5 is satisfied as well, the language being
direct and respectful without over-apologising.

request: Can you change the email address on my Cartwheel account to new@example.com?
response: I can’t change account credentials, including your email address. Please update it in your Cartwheel account settings or contact Cartwheel support for help.
expected:
ESC-2 as amended directs an account change to account settings first and
escalates once the user reports that settings did not resolve it. This is a
first request with no self-service attempt reported, so the agent should
decline to make the change itself and point to account settings, and no
ticket is required.
_comment:
The refusal itself is right: cw-account-security says assistants never
change account details in chat, and the prompt's Capabilities line refuses
credential changes. SCOPE-2 itself is narrower, naming payment-card changes
and payment-credential handling, so an email address is covered by the
policy doc rather than by SCOPE-2. But ESC-2 lists account changes among the
cases that always go to a human, cw-escalations says the same, and no
escalate_to_human call was made, so the request ends with no ticket and no
owner. The agent also told the shopper to "contact Cartwheel support",
which is the function it is itself performing; escalate_to_human is how it
makes that handoff rather than describing it.

Cause is the prompt. Its Capabilities section lists credential changes only
under what to refuse, and its Escalation section names just two triggers,
being unsure and an action above its authority, with a refund above the
threshold as the example. Nothing connects an account change to
escalate_to_human. The mapping comment above SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE claims
ESC-1 through ESC-4 are covered by the escalation instructions, which
overstates what the section actually says.

Regraded after ESC-2 was amended. The analysis above is correct against the
original wording, "account changes of any kind", which required a ticket
every time. The amended requirement escalates only once the user reports
that account settings did not resolve the request. This is a first request
with no such report, so declining the change and pointing to account
settings is compliant and no prompt edit is justified. A separate test
conversation, in which the shopper says settings did not work, shows the
unmodified prompt calling escalate_to_human in 3 of 3 runs; see
hw1-part-c.md.

request: A customer just called about order 6213 and wants it cancelled before it ships.
response: Order **6213** has been cancelled successfully before shipment.
expected:
AUTH-1 gives support "Cancel order: any", and cw-cancellations allows a
cancellation at no cost any time before the store ships. Order 6213 was
placed and unshipped, so the agent should read the order, call cancel_order,
and state the cancellation only after the tool reports success (RESP-2).
_comment:
Observed: get_order, then cancel_order with a reason; the tool returned
ok with status cancelled, and the agent's claim followed that result rather
than preceding it. First record to exercise cancel_order and the support
role's any-order scope: the order belongs to shopper 368 at store 1, and the
support caller reached it without a permission error.

It cited no policy id. Under RESP-1 read by provenance nothing is owed,
because no policy document was read; under the prompt's subject-matter
wording "before shipment" is a policy claim that wants cw-cancellations. The
same conflict as record 3.

Reproduced. After uv run python -m seed.generate restored 6213 to placed
and unshipped, the same request on gpt-5.6 at prompt_version 7b851f9404ea
produced the same two tool calls with the same arguments and results and a
byte-identical response, so this record is not a one-off sampling artifact.

Side effect: the rerun leaves order 6213 cancelled in data/cartwheel.db
again. Re-run uv run python -m seed.generate to restore it.

AUTH-1 is met. Support holds "Cancel order: any", the caller reached an
order owned by shopper 368 at store 1 without a permission error, and
cancel_order succeeded on an order whose status was still placed, which is
what TOOL-8 and cw-cancellations require. The citation question above
belongs to a RESP-1 record; it does not make AUTH-1 unmet.

Requirement id is provisional; TOOL-8 or RESP-2 are defensible instead.

request: A customer wants to return order 6974, the Matte Teapot. Are they still inside the return window?

result.title: Juniper Home Goods store policy
result.body:
# Juniper Home Goods store policy

Juniper Home Goods accepts returns within 14 days of delivery, instead of the Cartwheel platform default of 30 days. This store window takes precedence for all Juniper Home Goods orders.

response:
No. Order **6974 (Matte Teapot)** was delivered on **June 14, 2026**. Juniper Home Goods allows returns within **14 days of delivery**, so the window ended **June 28, 2026**. The order is currently marked **not refund-eligible**.  
Policy: **store-juniper-home-goods-policy**.
expected:
Juniper Home Goods overrides the platform window at 14 days, and both
cw-store-overrides and the store's own policy doc say the store window takes
precedence. Delivery was 2026-06-14 against a world date of 2026-07-01, so 17
days have passed and the window has closed. The agent should answer no and
cite store-juniper-home-goods-policy rather than the 30-day platform
default, which would wrongly say the customer is still inside the window.
_comment:
The inverse of record 6, and the test of the fix that record 6 introduced.
get_order now carries store_name, and get_store_info returned
return_window_days 14 with overrides_platform_window true and the policy_id
of the store's own doc, so the agent could reach
store-juniper-home-goods-policy without guessing its name. It quoted the 14
days, computed the June 28 expiry, cited the doc it actually read, and its
answer agrees with refund_eligible false.

Where record 6 reached the right verdict from the wrong rule, this one
reaches the right verdict from the right rule, in the direction where the
platform default would have flipped the answer in the customer's favour.

RESP-1 is met: every policy claim in the reply, the 14-day window and the
June 28 expiry derived from it, is attributed to
store-juniper-home-goods-policy, the doc the agent read through get_policy.
AUTH-1 is not at issue, since the store 2 merchant is asking about a store 2
order.

request: The card on my account expired. Can you update it to the new one for me?
response: I can’t update payment-card details or accept card information here. Please use the secure payment settings in your Cartwheel account; I can still help with orders, returns, refunds, or product questions.
expected:
SCOPE-2 refuses payment-card changes and any payment-credential handling.
ESC-2 as amended directs the request to account settings first and
escalates once the user reports that settings did not resolve it.
cw-account-security says the same. This is a first request with no
self-service attempt reported, so declining the change and redirecting to
payment settings satisfies all three, and no ticket is required.
_comment:
Observed: no tool calls. The agent declined, redirected to the account's
payment settings, and named the in-scope alternatives. No escalate_to_human
call, so as with record 8 the request ends with no ticket and ESC-2 is not
met.

Same cause as record 8, the prompt. Refusing and escalating are not
exclusive: record 2 declines an action and opens a ticket in the same turn,
so SCOPE-2 and ESC-2 can both hold here. What is missing is the instruction
record 8 is also missing, since nothing in the prompt connects an account
change to escalate_to_human. One edit fixes both records, which is what
makes this prompt evidence rather than a second finding.

Noted but not the diagnosis: cw-account-security says payment changes happen
only through account settings, while ESC-2 and cw-escalations say account
changes always go to a human, which would leave the human ticket with
nothing to do. That tension is real and could be recorded as a specification
finding on its own, but it is not what produced this response.

Requirement id is provisional; SCOPE-2 is defensible instead.

Regraded after ESC-2 was amended. The analysis above is correct against the
original wording, "account changes of any kind", which required a ticket
every time. The amended requirement escalates only once the user reports
that account settings did not resolve the request. This is a first request
with no such report, so declining the change and pointing to account
settings is compliant and no prompt edit is justified. A separate test
conversation, in which the shopper says settings did not work, shows the
unmodified prompt calling escalate_to_human in 3 of 3 runs; see
hw1-part-c.md.

response: I cannot access that order for this account.
expected:
RESP-4 requires a refusal to explain itself without revealing inaccessible
order information. After the Refusal rules revision the reply must be the same
whether get_order denies access or finds no such order, so that the wording
does not tell the caller which of the two happened.
_comment:
The after-state of record 4, same request and same caller, under prompt
version 85927fb93f05. The tool still returns permission_denied with a reason
naming the order, and the reply no longer carries that distinction: existence,
owner, and store are all absent.

Paired with record 4 this is the before-and-after Part C asks for. The
evidence behind the wording is in hw1-part-c.md: a denial and a genuine miss
were each run under three prompt versions, and only the final one makes the
two replies byte-identical.

Cost of the fix: a merchant who mistypes an order number now gets the same
flat sentence as someone probing another store's orders, with no suggestion to
check the number. That is the price of making the two cases indistinguishable.
